profile.reading:
CloudHQ MCC2 sits at 10100 Harry J Parish Boulevard, Manassas, Virginia, part of CloudHQ's MCC Campus, which the company's own current campus page describes as "CloudHQ's original campus location," on the south side of Manassas in Prince William County. A third-party data center aggregator separately reports 64 megawatts specifically for MCC2, a figure this profile notes as unconfirmed by the operator rather than adopting as fact. CloudHQ states the full MCC Campus totals 2,232,875 square feet and 382 megawatts of total critical IT load across seven data centers, with 96 megawatts currently available; the company's current site describes MCC5 as site-plan approved and ready for immediate development and MCC7's construction as beginning mid-2025 with an expected Q3 2026 ready-for-service date, but does not individually disclose MCC2's present-day capacity, so the campus total is not applied to this specific building. CloudHQ was founded in 2016 by Hossein Fateh, who also founded QTS Realty Trust and, per CloudHQ's own materials, was the first person in the United States to obtain an IRS ruling allowing data center income to qualify for real estate investment trust tax treatment. CloudHQ is privately held through the Fateh Family Office, with regional headquarters in Washington DC, London, and Singapore. CloudHQ does not name a power utility for the MCC Campus on its current site.

Prince William County's Manassas-area data center corridor has grown alongside Loudoun County's much larger Ashburn cluster, though the two submarkets have followed somewhat different zoning and community-engagement trajectories; Prince William County has seen significant public debate in recent years over large-scale data center rezoning proposals near residential areas and historic sites, though this profile does not confirm CloudHQ's MCC Campus specifically as a party to any particular zoning controversy without independent sourcing. CloudHQ's global portfolio spans 23 campuses and more than 30 million square feet across six countries, with more than 1,380 megawatts of critical IT load already contracted company-wide.

reading.body:
CloudHQ MCC2 is part of a 2.2 million square foot campus in Northern Virginia with no published power capacity, making its significance to AI infrastructure impossible to rank against disclosed facilities.

The campus footprint is large enough to matter. At conventional data center densities, 2.2 million square feet typically corresponds to somewhere between 335 MW and 500 MW of IT load, depending on how densely equipment is packed. At AI training densities of 40 kW per rack, the space could hold roughly 8,000 racks. At colocation densities around 10 kW per rack, it could hold four times that. These are not operator claims but industry benchmarks applied to physical footprint.

What remains unknown is whether this campus is actually built out at those densities, or at all. The operator publishes technical space and mentions that 96 MW of critical load capacity was available as of mid-2025, and that construction on additional buildings was planned. Without a published total IT load figure, the facility cannot be compared directly to Virginia's 19 disclosing sites, which average 70 MW each. The absence of certified compliance profiles means no statement can be made about whether this campus is configured for AI workloads specifically.

For compute scaling, what matters is deployed power, not zoned square footage. This facility demonstrates that large real estate exists in Northern Virginia's data center corridor, but whether it will become binding infrastructure for AI depends entirely on build-out decisions the operator has not yet made public.
